story_text.value:
Hi HN, I wanted to take a stance on these topics people have been arguing all around. There should be some sort of answer, right?

I used to go to debates for that end. But I often only see the repetition of the same points, the hardest objection being dodged, etc. I tried AI as well, but it only returns surface level arguments likewise.

Is there anyway to preserve debate's purpose in trying to see the deepest case, while getting over these “sophistry”?

Could I map all the arguments in controversial topics (continuously allowing new inputs), and rephrase and put them in a clear sequence, so fallacies, detours, and claims already have well-established answers could be cleared out, leaving only the real tradeoff standing?

I tried it: creating TruthTree (Truthtree.app). Anything it has missed, you can hit "Challenge this claim”, type your counter, and if it's spot on (through the AI, with a fallback checker), it will be on the tree.

For example, for abortion, the map currently filters out this unanswered crux: "knowingly creating a life that depends on your body gives you a duty to continue the pregnancy."(https://truthtree.app/abortion/responsibility)

Is that the answer to abortion? What’s the map missing?

Please also let me know if this format works, and if there’s anything that could be changed to make things easier!

title.value: Ask HN: Can I map all the arguments in a topic to "approach the truth"?

story_text.value:
Hi all,

Recently, Opus 5.5 and I as lowly Director in Chief (but I still feel like I matter, and that I'm good enough and smart enough to be involved, doggone it!), revamped this LR clone with procedural levels/music (it already had that, this was just a broad improvement/enhancement pass). It was ok'ish before but after the overhaul I was kind of taken back with how playable and good it is now.

Added multiplayer and playing on a TV (Android/Google TV app and should work with a paired BT controller).

It's pretty fun I have to say. I get bored with most LR's after a bit but this one I actually want to keep playing. It's unique (I think) with the seeded procedural unlimited levels and procedural synth music, and also you can choose Soma Space Station streaming radio for the music which usually fits in perfectly. And it has some added touches like a piece of red outlined gold that you cannot reach and can only get from an AI whose captured it etc, and you can change the difficulty to pretty insane levels. Normal mode is already challenging.

A little tech/stack info: All game rules are now implemented using a TypeScript simulation environment that is separate from Phaser. This allows use of the exact same logic to render the game, run tests against the game, and verify that the levels created by the level generation system are valid and complete enough. The level creation process uses a solver to analyze possible movements and digging actions that a player could take, and verifies that a level can actually be completed.

Built w TypeScript, Phaser 4, and Vite (client), Go server that handles the web app and the TV/phone-controller connection.

I think it's performant enough, but not sure if the stack/architecture could be rethought to make it faster and lighter and less potential lag on lower end devices etc. This is basically vibe-coded, I'm more a Linux/ops guy than a developer or programmer.

Feedback welcomed.

https://loderunner2099.exe.xyz https://loderunner2099.exe.xyz/tv https://loderunner2099.exe.xyz/app https://loderunner2099.exe.xyz/pad

story_text.value:
Hi HN, I'm Frank, founder of Truce.

Truce is a neutral AI mediator. Each side tells it their side in private, Truce proposes one specific outcome, and nothing happens unless both people sign.

The part that may interest you is the agent side. Truce is a remote MCP server (https://trucehq.com/mcp) with 12 tools, so an assistant can start a Truce for its user, or answer one for the other person with their consent.

There is also "Agent Truce": two agents acting for different people or companies settle a dispute between themselves, such as a refund, a late delivery or an invoice. Each agent gives its side, its evidence and a private mandate from its human, for example "may pay up to $300". The mediator never sees either mandate, so it proposes on the merits. A proposal that fits inside both mandates is accepted automatically; anything else goes back to the humans. Truce never moves money.

It's free for AI agents. One-minute demo on the page.

I'd especially like criticism of the mandate design. How would you game it, and what would make you trust it for your own agents?

story_text.value:
Two years ago, I tried making a sudoku game in React, but I let it go because getting everything properly implemented turned out to be quite a bit of work. Then AI came along. I’ve spent the past few weeks working hard on Klink in the evenings and on weekends.

It started out with experimenting a Tamagotchi-style game where you had to take care of a little robot and gradually add more parts to it. But it turned out that a Tamagotchi on an iPhone didn’t really work, I was just mashing buttons and it didn't give me that same feeling I got as a kid clicking the little buttons to feed my pixelated friend. I then thought of a talk given by Theo (the T3 Youtuber) about how we should all think bigger when working with AI and I’ve always wanted to make a sudoku game. So that got me thinking about the sudoku games/apps I played in the past.

I’ve always found sudoku games a bit dry. Other than a "Daily Challenge" there isn't really an incentive to have me coming back and then after a few days I forget all about it. So I started with prompting and kept prompting and prompting until I’d built a sudoku app that was actually usable, with one extra mechanic: building and upgrading a little robot. The flow of the game is that you solve a puzzle, this gives you scrap, that scrap is then used to "buy" new components, or upgrade existing components. (each component has Mk I, Mk II, Mk III versions)

I'm Dutch and it's Sinterklaas season here, so I added an in-game event where you can earn robot parts themed around the holiday. They're only available during this time of the year. Up next will probably be Christmas.

Alongside classic sudoku, I added quite a few variants (Killer, Thermo, Sandwich, Arrows, Diagonal, Chaos (Jigsaw), Kropki, Even/Odd, Hyper, Binaro, and Trees and Tents). I also added “Tricks,” which are basically short lessons on how to use standard sudoku techniques and recognize patterns. Then I polished the app a bit more and finally released it to the App Store last Friday. You can play it on iOS, iPadOS, and macOS.

Since Friday, I’ve had a whopping 15 downloads, mostly from friends and family (to be honest, probably all of them). I also made a website: https://klinksudoku.com. Normally I just work as a developer at a company and this is my first time I actually have to think about things like marketing, getting more users, promoting the product which is very fun to experience.

Currently I’m also looking for Android testers. Since I have a personal developer account, Google requires me to have 12 people in a closed test before I can release the app publicly. You can join the test group here: https://groups.google.com/g/klink-sudoku-testers

I’m curious what you think.

title.value: Show HN: Klink – I built a sudoku game where every puzzle helps rebuild a robot

story_text.value:
It seems to me the industry is at a divergence point, with strong forces pull in opposite directions.

In the "developers are team leads / checkpoint verifiers" corner we have:

- Microsoft, re "They build a software factory that builds the product. They don’t build the product" (Nadella) and "become a manager of agents, rather than a person directly doing the work" <https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/18/microsoft-ceo-satya-nadella-explains-why-he-asked-60k-employees-to-quit/>

-- Microsoft has always championed "AI as a team member", even as a product.

- Salesforce <https://www.salesforce.com/news/stories/how-engineering-became-agentic/>

- Stripe <https://stripe.dev/blog/minions-stripes-one-shot-end-to-end-coding-agents>

- Uber, Shopify, Spotify, Meta

In the "developers use harnesses to improve personal velocity and quality corner we have:

- Netflix <https://qconsf.com/presentation/nov2026/how-netflix-retrofitted-its-sdlc-ai-coding-agents>

- Amazon <https://www.aboutamazon.com/news/company-news/amazon-software-engineer-role-guideline-ai>

- ... Google, but it's hard to find more than anecdotal references

These two approaches, in my view, are not compatible. Fully, or even just semi-automated feature factories keep the context, leaving the developer to validate artifacts and manage the flow, shifting responsibility to specs and building automated verifiers. It lets less technical people into the product development loop but keeps the code an AI-only territory.

On the other hand, a harness keeps the developer in control, but sacrifices velocity and requires higher technical prowess, or at least understanding, of what's being generated.

Which way is the industry going to go? Are AI-only maintained code bases going to collapse under their own weight? Are "technical" developers going to be sidelined for higher delivery velocity? Will we see two types of businesses - features and infra, each taking a polar position in this? Or even within the same business, different teams?

title.value: Ask HN: Harness vs. Feature Factories

story_text.value: Hello, i am sharing a concern/opinion that i’ve been contemplating for the past couple of years. Today, we see how vibe coders with plain-english are building basic websites/webapps/mobile apps etc… you name it. Most of it is being used for good. Setting aside the quality, slop and everything else, this is not our concern. For me, the AI/agentic systems surge, directly empowered another group of people: Hackers, regardless of their nature (black hat, white hat etc…). Similar to software engineers, hackers required an immensive amount of theoretical knowledge, practical expertise and years of experience in order to be market ready (whether for an actual job or not). Script-kiddies as we know them, weren’t that meticulous in their craft , they understood some basics and executed pre-defined scripts. They didnt know how to change them, alter them or even create some their own. But today, in our new agentic-era, I believe English is the only requirement alongside a target. Considering the LLM being used is jailbroken/not safeguarded and restricted, they can literally break into systems, easily. So I was thinking to myself, a lot of people wanted to be hackers but they couldn’t (it required effort in studying, practicing etc…), today it doesnt need the same amount of effort anymore. So in the future, we are definitely going to see a surge in the number of hackers. The question comes here: How are we going to defend against malicious activities? Do we have AI-Powered systems that could act like a security analyst? Forensics? And how powerful are they? Are they deployed in reputable companies? How are they performing? Vibe-hackers are now stronger than ever, defense is required. Whether at org level or for individuals.

title.value: Vibe-Hackers: Script kiddies, stronger?

story_text.value:
As somebody that is not a natural learning languages, I found it really hard to get enough practise to feel confident speaking when you actually have someone to talk to someone. I wanted somewhere to practise everyday conversation out lout, so I made Maido.

It's a free game in your browser and works on desktop or mobile with nothing to install and no login or account needed. You can even sync progress between your devices via an encrypted blind relay by using a QR code.

Each language has a 3D town where you walk around, talk to people with your mic (or by typing) and run ordinary errands like ordering food, buying flowers, getting groceries, and talking with neighbours. Each place has a number of districts you can travel around and a story unfolds as you go along. The characters answer in their own language with life like voices, with translations and explanations tailored to the skill level you are on.

Open-ended conversations use hosted AI (I'm paying for this out of pocket). There is a 10 minute allowance per day to keep it manageable. Once that runs out, the scripted engine kicks in, or you can BYOK with your own (free) Gemini API key. This also unlocks Gemini Live mode where the response is nearly instant. There are no ads or payments at the moment.

For the TLDR crowd, I've been learning Japanese for a very long time so Yunagi is the flagship town. You can jump to it directly here - https://maido.place/yunagi/

I'll make a longer post below on how it's built and more technical bits. Would love any feedback, bug reports, etc. on https://github.com/nyblnet/maido-community or hello@maido.place

story_text.value:
Hi HN, I'm Nadia, one of the makers of CadYam. My cofounder Jared is here to answer questions as well.

CadYam is a desktop design app built for a person and an AI agent to work on the same project: a CAD drawing, a video, an interior design plan, a data analysis, etc. You can sketch something by asking it to your agent and drop a pin on a specific place to ask for changes.

We built this after a lot of frustration trying to learn traditional CAD tools, which have a steep learning curve and take a lot of time and effort before you can build anything complex. With CadYam, the agent can do the work for you with your guidance or teach you how to use the app if you'd like to do some manual work yourself, so you also don't always need the agent.

The agent's changes show up as a preview you iterate on with natural language. No technical skills required to use it. You can watch a short demo (under a minute) at https://youtu.be/NbA28Pshxyo or click around some demo exports in your browser without installing anything: https://codeyam-ai.github.io/cadyam-exports/

We were also inspired by the HN threads about creative tools rebuilt in Rust, e.g. discussed in this HN thread: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49959605

Some technical details:

- CadYam is written in Rust and runs a local MCP server. Agents connect to it and use the same commands you do, so they can drive almost everything in the app. CadYam has instructions for connecting a range of agents.

- We built CadYam with CodeYam (codeyam.com), a product we developed for building software with AI. It lets us develop quickly while keeping the app well organized and well tested. We're shipping about two dozen fixes and features a day (more than 600 in the last month), so feature suggestions and bug reports are welcome and should get fixed quickly.

- The app is currently free for macOS, Windows, and Linux. It probably won't be free forever, but if we do charge, it will be a small amount. It's inexpensive for us to develop, and it doubles as a demo of what you can build with CodeYam.

We'd love for you to try it and share your feedback.

title.value: Show HN: A free creative suite, built in Rust, for AI collaboration

story_text.value:
Hey everyone, I'm Steven. I wanted to share a new project we're working on called Wyrd. It's a real-time verification platform for AI systems. Whether it's AI or standard services, every team uses a variety of tools to determine if their systems are working as expected. However, there tends to be a dearth of tools/platforms that can do this in real-time. From our perspective, as AI is used more and more to make autonomous decisions, there should be more emphasis on real-time verification. So we built Wyrd, which provides you and your teams all of the primitives to build your own real-time verification workflows. Would love for interested people to kick it around, provide feedback and contribute.

url: https://github.com/bohmian-ai/wyrd license: Apache 2.0
